prompt: One of the oldest α-amino acid syntheses begins with α bromination of a carboxylic acid (the Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii reaction). What reagents carry out this bromination?

choices.why: The book's α bromination of a carboxylic acid uses Br2 and PBr3, the Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii conditions.
The Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii reaction uses Br2 and PBr3.
NaBH4 and NH3 are used in reductive amination of α-keto acids, not α bromination.

explanation: α-Amino acids can be made by α bromination of a carboxylic acid with Br2 and PBr3 (the Hell–Volhard–Zelinskii reaction), followed by S_N2 substitution of the α-bromo acid with ammonia.

prompt: In Knowles's enantioselective hydrogenation, (S)-phenylalanine is obtained at 98.7% purity. What percent of the product is the (R) enantiomer?
explanation: The book reports that (S)-phenylalanine is prepared at 98.7% purity, contaminated by only 1.3% of the (R) enantiomer (100% − 98.7% = 1.3%), when a chiral rhodium catalyst is used.

prompt: Which carboxylic acid is the starting material for the book's synthesis of leucine by α bromination followed by reaction with ammonia?

choices.why: 3-Methylbutanoic acid gives valine by this route (Exercise 26.3.1).
3-Phenylpropanoic acid gives phenylalanine by this route (Exercise 26.3.1).
The α carbon must end up bearing H, so the branch is on carbon 4: 4-methylpentanoic acid.

explanation: 4-Methylpentanoic acid reacts with Br2 and PBr3 to give 2-bromo-4-methylpentanoic acid, which reacts with excess ammonia to give (R,S)-leucine.

prompt: In the book's synthesis of (R,S)-leucine from 2-bromo-4-methylpentanoic acid and excess ammonia, what percent yield of leucine is obtained?
explanation: The book reports that 2-bromo-4-methylpentanoic acid reacts with excess ammonia to form (R,S)-leucine in 45% yield.

prompt: Which carboxylic acid would you start with to make phenylalanine by treatment with 1. Br2, PBr3; 2. NH3?

choices.why: That acid has only one carbon between the ring and the carboxyl; bromination and amination would give an amino acid with the phenyl on the α carbon.
This acid has one CH2 too many; phenylalanine's side chain is a single CH2 attached to the phenyl group.
3-Methylbutanoic acid gives valine.

explanation: Exercise 26.3.1: phenylalanine, C6H5CH2CH(NH2)CO2H, comes from 3-phenylpropanoic acid, C6H5CH2CH2CO2H. α Bromination with Br2 and PBr3 followed by NH3 puts the amino group on carbon 2.

prompt: Which carboxylic acid would you start with to make valine by treatment with 1. Br2, PBr3; 2. NH3?

choices.why: 4-Methylpentanoic acid gives leucine, whose side chain has an extra CH2.
This acid's α carbon already carries two methyl groups; the amino group would end up on a carbon with no hydrogen.
Butanoic acid has an unbranched chain; valine's side chain is an isopropyl group.

explanation: Exercise 26.3.1: valine, (CH3)2CHCH(NH2)CO2H, comes from 3-methylbutanoic acid, (CH3)2CHCH2CO2H, by α bromination (Br2, PBr3) and then S_N2 reaction with NH3.

prompt: Which sequence describes the amidomalonate synthesis of an α-amino acid?

choices.text: Alkylate the enolate of diethyl acetamidomalonate, then warm with aqueous acid
Brominate a carboxylic acid with Br2 and PBr3, then substitute with ammonia
choices.why: That is the older route through α-bromo acids, not the amidomalonate synthesis.

choices.text: Treat an α-keto acid with ammonia and NaBH4 to reduce the imine
choices.why: That is reductive amination of an α-keto acid.

choices.text: Hydrogenate a Z enamido acid with a chiral rhodium catalyst
choices.why: That is Knowles's enantioselective synthesis.

explanation: The amidomalonate synthesis extends the malonic ester synthesis. Diethyl acetamidomalonate is converted into an enolate with base, then alkylated by S_N2 reaction with a primary alkyl halide. Warming with aqueous acid hydrolyzes the amide protecting group and the esters, and decarboxylation then gives the α-amino acid.

prompt: What alkyl halide does the book use to make aspartic acid by the amidomalonate synthesis?

choices.why: This secondary halide would put a methyl branch next to the α carbon; aspartic acid's side chain is simply –CH2CO2H.
This halide adds one CH2 too many; aspartic acid's side chain is –CH2CO2H.
Bromomethane would give the side chain –CH3, which is alanine.

explanation: Aspartic acid is prepared from diethyl acetamidomalonate, sodium ethoxide, and ethyl bromoacetate, BrCH2CO2Et. Heating the resulting triester with aqueous acid gives (R,S)-aspartic acid in 55% yield.

prompt: In the book's amidomalonate synthesis of aspartic acid from ethyl bromoacetate, what percent yield of (R,S)-aspartic acid is obtained?
explanation: Diethyl acetamidomalonate is alkylated with ethyl bromoacetate (using sodium ethoxide as base), and heating the triester with aqueous acid gives (R,S)-aspartic acid in 55% yield.

prompt: What alkyl halide would you use to prepare leucine by the amidomalonate method?

choices.why: This would give the isopropyl side chain of valine, and it is a secondary halide.
This gives an unbranched butyl side chain; leucine's side chain is an isobutyl group.
This tertiary halide doesn't undergo S_N2 alkylation, and its group isn't leucine's side chain.

explanation: In the amidomalonate synthesis the alkyl halide supplies the side chain. Leucine's side chain is –CH2CH(CH3)2, an isobutyl group, so the halide is 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (Exercise 26.3.2).

prompt: What alkyl halide would you use to prepare methionine by the amidomalonate method?

choices.why: This gives the side chain –CH2SCH3, one CH2 short of methionine's –CH2CH2SCH3.
This would give the side chain –CH2SH, which is cysteine.
This gives a propyl side chain with no sulfur.

explanation: Methionine's side chain is –CH2CH2SCH3, so the alkyl halide is the bromoethyl methyl thioether, CH3SCH2CH2Br (Exercise 26.3.2).

prompt: Applying the amidomalonate method, which alkyl halide would give phenylalanine?

choices.why: This gives no CH2 between the ring and the α carbon, and an aryl halide doesn't undergo S_N2 reactions.
This would give the side chain –CH2CH2C6H5, one CH2 too many.
Ethyl bromoacetate gives aspartic acid.

explanation: The amidomalonate synthesis alkylates the enolate with a primary alkyl halide that supplies the side chain. Phenylalanine's side chain is –CH2C6H5, so benzyl bromide, C6H5CH2Br, is the halide to use.

prompt: How is alanine prepared by reductive amination?

choices.text: Pyruvic acid is treated with ammonia and NaBH4; an intermediate imine forms and is reduced
Pyruvic acid is treated with Br2 and PBr3, then with ammonia
choices.why: Br2 and PBr3 brominate the α carbon of a carboxylic acid; reductive amination uses NH3 and a reducing agent on an α-keto acid.

choices.text: Propanoic acid is treated with ammonia and NaBH4; an intermediate enamine forms
choices.why: Reductive amination starts from an α-keto acid, pyruvic acid, and goes through an imine.

choices.text: Pyruvic acid is treated with ammonia alone, which displaces the ketone oxygen in an S_N2 reaction
choices.why: A reducing agent is needed: the ketone and ammonia form an imine, which NaBH4 reduces.

explanation: Reductive amination of an α-keto acid with ammonia and a reducing agent gives an α-amino acid. Alanine is prepared by treating pyruvic acid with ammonia in the presence of NaBH4; the reaction goes through an intermediate imine, which is then reduced.

prompt: What is obtained when an α-amino acid is made from an achiral precursor by α bromination and amination, the amidomalonate synthesis, or reductive amination?

choices.text: A racemic mixture of the S and R enantiomers
Only the S enantiomer, the one found in proteins
choices.why: These methods have no chiral influence, so they give both enantiomers equally; the book labels the products (R,S).

choices.text: Only the R enantiomer, the nonnatural one
choices.why: Nothing in these methods favors one enantiomer; both form in equal amounts.

choices.text: Mostly the S enantiomer, about 98.7% S
choices.why: That kind of excess needs an enantioselective method such as Knowles's chiral rhodium catalyst.

explanation: Synthesis of an α-amino acid from an achiral precursor by any of these methods yields a racemic mixture. To make a natural protein, the pure S enantiomer is needed, obtained either by resolution or by enantioselective synthesis.

prompt: In Knowles's enantioselective synthesis, (S)-phenylalanine is made at 98.7% purity. How?

choices.text: By hydrogenating a Z enamido acid with a chiral rhodium catalyst
By hydrogenating a Z enamido acid with an achiral palladium catalyst
choices.why: An achiral catalyst would give a racemic product; the chiral rhodium catalyst holds the substrate in a chiral environment.

choices.text: By resolving racemic phenylalanine into its enantiomers
choices.why: Resolution is the other way to get pure enantiomers; Knowles's method makes the S enantiomer directly.

choices.text: By reductive amination of an α-keto acid with NaBH4
choices.why: Reductive amination with NaBH4 gives a racemic product.

explanation: William Knowles at Monsanto discovered in 1968 that α-amino acids can be prepared enantioselectively by hydrogenating a Z enamido acid with a chiral hydrogenation catalyst. With a chiral rhodium catalyst, (S)-phenylalanine is formed at 98.7% purity, with only 1.3% of the (R) enantiomer. The best catalysts are rhodium(I) complexes with COD and a chiral diphosphine such as DiPAMP, which is chiral because of its trisubstituted phosphorus atoms.
